In PKLD and all of its known descendants other than Sa'ban stress is penultimate. In Sa'ban, as just noted, it is generally final, but may be marginally phonemic, depending upon the interpretation of extrametrical schwa in the sequences -/ieC/ and -/ueC/. [pp.260-261:] First, it retains a contrast between *a, *i and *u in prepenultimate (pretonic) syllables. ... new_statements.rule_in_words: Per Blust 2001, all Kelabit-Lun Dayeh (PKLD) descendants except Sa'ban -- a class in which he explicitly places Long Terawan Tring -- have penultimate word stress. BUT Blust's own 1971 field transcriptions of Tring (notebook RB2-003-A pp.23-27, saved) mark stress on the final syllable of every polysyllabic citation form, and Blust 2006:315 (quoted by Mortensen 2021:52) describes N. Sarawak stress as final in citation forms but penultimate in phrasal context, near-even in Kelabit/Lun Dayeh. So: penult by the author's generalization, final in his citation-form data; no Tring-specific published sentence was accessible.
new_statements.exceptions: Sa'ban (final stress, marginally phonemic with extrametrical schwa in -ieC/-ueC) is the stated exception within KLD; nothing Tring-specific.
new_statements.domain_note: The 2001 statement is a family-level typological generalization, not a description of Tring; the conflicting notebook evidence is citation forms elicited from a single speaker (George Bidui) in one session. Likely reconciliation (Blust 2006 via Mortensen): final prominence in citation forms vs penultimate in phrasal context; unverified for Tring. The Tring-specific phonology paragraph is in Blust 1984 SMJ sec. 1, not accessible online.
new_statements.identity_note: All modern data are for the Tring dialect of Long Terawan (Tutoh River, Baram, Sarawak; one speaker, George Bidui, recorded by Blust in 1971), which Blust classes as a Kelabit(-Lun Dayeh) dialect; Glottolog trin1273 / ISO tgq. Ray 1913's 'Treng' covers Balait and Tabun (and Long Pata, which Ray himself says is a Lower Baram language, not Dayic). Note the our source list lat/lon (1.335, 110.036) points to western Sarawak, far from Long Terawan (~3.9N 114.6E) -- likely a Glottolog coordinate issue, not a different language.

Blust's own 1971 Tring citation forms are consistently ticked on the FINAL syllable, which is the opposite placement at the level of citation forms. The two are reconcilable through Blust's later remark (Blust 2006 OL 45:315 as quoted by Mortensen 2021:52, held by the project under kela1258) that northern Sarawak languages show final stress in citation forms but penultimate stress in phrasal context; the notebook is entirely citation-form elicitation. new_statements.rule_in_words: No statement about stress anywhere on the Tring pages: the notebook is a 203-item elicited wordlist plus kinship terms and a to-check list. Blust's stress tick (ˈ) is written before the FINAL syllable of every polysyllabic citation form that carries a tick (numerals, body parts, verbs, nouns, adjectives, trisyllables such as bəpiˈkil, səluˈbit, ləmuˈlun, təmaˈlut, təməˈčul, kədaˈluh); I found no form ticked on the penult. The tick is a genuine per-word record and not a mechanical habit: the same notebook's Long Anap Kenyah list (p.41, image 020) mixes penult ticks ('ləma, 'piʔən, 'puloʔ, 'takut, 'likut, 'tulay, 'tisən) with final ones. So the primary data show final stress on Tring citation forms as heard by Blust in 1971. The notebook's Narum pages (p.21, image 010) carry the reminder 'Check stress in citation forms and in context', showing Blust was already tracking a citation-vs-phrase difference in this fieldwork. The listed audio (RB1-003, hdl:10125/4681) was not downloaded: it is sound only, its item metadata lists languages kyi, ttw, snv, sib, zbe (no tgq), is dated '[1990s?]', and the 'Long Terawan' track is more likely Berawan of Long Terawan than Tring. The hi-res zips RB2-003-A-1.5.zip are 115-313 MB each, all above the 80 MB cap, so only the low-res scans were used.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing; single tick per word only.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated. Several polysyllables carry no tick at all (limah ~ dimah '5', siwaʔ '9', bulan 'moon', the pronoun forms kəduah, kətəluh, məduah on p.26, most kinship terms on p.27); these are unmarked, not counter-marked.
new_statements.identity_note: The notebook pages are headed 'Treng Tring, Oct. 18' with the query 'Is the name of this lg. Treng or Tring?' on p.27; the variety is the Tring of Long Terawan (Tutoh, Baram), ISO tgq = trin1273, the same variety Blust 1984 and 2001 treat. The audio item RB1-003 'Long Terawan' (side 2 track 1) is tagged with kyi, ttw, snv, sib, zbe and no tgq, so it is probably Berawan of Long Terawan, not Tring; it was not downloaded (audio, no text). The notebook's Long Anap (Kenyah, p.41) and Narum (p.21) pages were used only as controls for Blust's tick notation.

readall_conflicts: The only Tring-specific primary source, Blust's 1971 field notebook RB2-003-A pp.23-27, transcribes every stress-ticked polysyllabic citation form with final stress (duˈah, təˈluh, puˈluʔ, tuˈlaŋ, bəpiˈkil, ləmuˈlun, təmaˈlut, kədaˈluh..), whereas the catalog's penultimate rule rests on Blust 2001:267, a family-level statement that all PKLD descendants except Sa'ban have penultimate stress (Tring enters only by membership in Kelabit, Table 1 p.254, p.271). Blust 2006:315 (via Mortensen 2021:52) supplies the likely reconciliation: northern Sarawak languages have final stress in citation forms and penultimate stress in phrasal context, and the notebook is citation-form elicitation only; the notebook's own Narum page (p.21) carries the reminder 'Check stress in citation forms and in context'. No source gives a Tring-specific prose rule; Blust 1984 (Sarawak Museum Journal 33:101-135), which presumably does, is print-only (only its first two pages are online).
